item.title: Forgiveness: Bible Verses to Help You Forgive
item.description:
Forgiveness is a topic that sounds easy enough in principle but often feels impossible to put into practice. I remember the grief I felt years ago when the missionary organization I was serving painted me as sexually immoral, sent an email to every religious authority in the small country I was serving in to beware of me, and then let me go with zero proof of actual “sin,” and zero chance for me to defend myself.

This baseless spiritual abuse nearly drove me away from God. It took years before I could forgive my accusers.

We all know the pain of unforgiveness. The one that keeps us awake at night. The one that twists inside us like a knife. How can we extend forgiveness when the person we’re angry with has done the unthinkable? Doesn’t God know what they did to us? How then can He demand we forgive them?

Neuroscience of Resentment

Before we dive into Scripture, I’d like to point out that there are scientific reasons to back up God’s wisdom when it comes to forgiveness. We all know that refusing to forgive an offense can spiral into resentment and bitterness.

As shown in neuro scans studying the effects of unforgiveness, “[r]esentment creates a self-perpetuating cycle (Clark, 2005, as cited in Cherry, n.d.). When you replay what happened, you reactivate the same neural pathways, strengthening the emotional intensity of the memory through long-term potentiation (Kumar, 2011, as cited in Cherry, n.d.).”

This means that the more you ruminate on an event, the more it gets reinforced in your brain’s neural networks, leaving you stuck in the past and secreting cortisol, the stress hormone. Over time, the constant secretion of cortisol and the hyperarousal of the amygdala due to unresolved stress lead to depression, anxiety, and lower self-worth.

“Unforgiveness also correlates with sleep disturbances, cardiovascular problems, elevated blood pressure, weakened immune function, and increased inflammation markers (Abohashem et al., 2024 as cited in Cherry, n.d.; Segerstrom & Miller, 2004 as cited in Cherry, n.d.).”

Rumination leads to cortisol buildup over time. This is due to chronic stress. “Chronic stress causes the muscles in the body to be in a more or less constant state of guardedness. When muscles are taut and tense for long periods of time, this may trigger other reactions of the body and even promote stress-related disorders” (American Psychological Association, 2024).

These stress-related disorders include migraines or chronic headaches because of muscle tension in the neck, shoulders, and head. There are several more systems in the body that get triggered, including the endocrine system, HPA axis, gastrointestinal system, among others (Ibid). Needless to say, unforgiveness is a life stressor that can have far greater consequences than one might expect.

God, creator of the human body, knew this well before the advances of Western medicine. This is why He is so clear in Scripture that forgiveness is essential, not only physically, but spiritually as well. But what exactly does God mean by forgiveness?

What Biblical Forgiveness Is

The purpose of this article is not to use Scripture as a shaming device for those struggling to forgive. There’s a wide misconception about what biblical forgiveness means and what our Western culture makes it out to be. We often think God is asking us to forgive and forget, restore the full trust we had before the offense, or even excuse bad behavior. This is not what the Bible teaches.

If your brother sins against you, go and tell his fault, between you and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained your brother. But if he does not listen, take one or two others along with you, that every charge may be established by the evidence of two or three witnesses. If he refuses to listen to them, tell it to the church. And if he refuses to listen even to the church, let him be to you as a Gentile and a tax collector. – Matt. 18:15-17, ESV

Let’s take a closer look at what Jesus is saying in this passage. By using the word “brother,” He’s speaking of a person in the church, i.e., a Christian. Jesus advocates for private reconciliation between Christians wherever possible. He also makes it clear that He’s not speaking of trivial charges, but those of serious merit that can be corroborated by two or three witnesses.

The Greek word used in Matt. 18:15 is a variant of the word hamartánō, which is an archer’s term for missing the mark. A deeper dive into the word explains, “properly, having no share in; to sin, which always brings forfeiture – i.e., eternal loss due to missing God’s mark” (Strong’s Greek: 264).

If this Christian “brother” has refused to reconcile privately despite ample evidence of their wrongdoing, only then should it be brought before a spiritual body. If the offender does not listen to the church and witnesses, they are considered an unbeliever, and thus an outsider to the congregation.

The individual initially seeking reconciliation is also instructed to see them the same way. This denotes removing the closeness and the trust the offender held formerly.

Let’s be clear. Jesus isn’t saying, “Don’t forgive.” By making the offender an outsider of the church, Jesus is providing a way for shame to lead the offender to repentance. Once again, Jesus’ goal is for repentance and forgiveness between Christians, not for Christians to hold grudges or remove fellow believers from the church. Removal from the church is a means to bring the offender to repentance.

Forgiveness is further demonstrated in Matt. 18:21-22, where it says, “Then Peter came up and said to him, ‘Lord, how often will my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? As many as seven times?’ Jesus said to him, ‘I do not say to you seven times, but seventy times seven’ (ESV). Jesus asks that we forgive indefinitely. But once again, if the brother doesn’t repent, He’s not asking us to be pushovers.

If we focused solely on these passages, we might think God only asks us to forgive other Christians. But that’s not what’s implied in Matt. 5:44 when Jesus says, “But I say to you, love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you” (ESV). Paul gives a full description of what it means to love in 1 Corinthians 13.

In 1 Cor. 13:5, love is described as keeping no account of wrongs. The word used is the Greek logizetai. “The term appears in moral contexts where believers weigh motives and actions: 1 Corinthians 13:5: love keeps no account of wrongs;” it does not keep a mental ledger for retaliation (Strong’s Greek: 3049).

So, to love enemies is to keep no account, i.e., no ledger of the wrongs they’ve done against us. The antidote to our vindictiveness toward enemies is given in the same verse in Matt. 5:44, when Jesus tells us to pray for them. By praying for them, we are leaving God room to work on the hearts of our persecutors and replacing bitterness in ourselves with loving, restorative action.

Jesus doesn’t stop with asking us to forgive our brothers (Christians) or enemies (persecutors). He also asks us to love our “neighbor,” which again implies keeping no record of their wrongs. This is evident in Mark 12:31 when Jesus says, “The second [commandment] is this: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ There is no other commandment greater than these” (ESV).

Neighbors, as we know from urban living, can be anyone – a Christian, an enemy, a non-Christian, even a complete stranger. Jesus’ command for forgiveness is thus universal. We are to forgive everyone regardless of their believing status.

Two further verses that back this up are Ephesians 4:32: Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you (Ibid), and Colossians 3:13: “[Bear] with one another and, if one has a complaint against another, [forgive] each other; as the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive” (ESV).

The Commandment to Forgive

Forgiveness is a command. Notice again in Colossians 3:13 where it states, “as the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive.” (ESV, emphasis added)

We don’t get a free pass here. Even if we’re angry, even if the offense was great, even if we’re still hurting, we must forgive. Jesus doubles down on this in Matt. 6:14-15 when he says, “For if you forgive others their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you, but if you do not forgive others their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses (ESV).”

Paul tells us in Romans 12:18-21: If possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all. Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God, for it is written, “Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord.” To the contrary, “if your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him something to drink; for by so doing, you will heap burning coals on his head.” Do not be overcome by evil but overcome evil with good (ESV).

Conclusion

God doesn’t want us to ruminate. He doesn’t want the chronic stress of unforgiveness to destroy us. He calls us to action. Love our enemies. Pray for them. Do good to them. Feed them. Quench their thirst. Leave God to choose how He wishes to respond to their wrongdoing. There’s so much wisdom in these commands. Psychologically, action is infinitely more healing than inaction.

Forgiveness is a process. We aren’t expected to instantly be okay with what happened to us. With God’s help and our obedience, forgiveness is possible. Even when it feels anything but.

item.title: Peacekeepers and the Codependency Symptoms Nobody Talks About
item.description:
Those of us who carry the peacekeeper role do not think of it as a role at all. We see it as part of how we function, stepping in before the argument starts or keeping the mood in the room from shifting. We give a little more than is comfortable for us, so that no one else has to feel uncomfortable. This always looks like kindness from the outside, and it comes from a genuinely caring place.

There are times when giving never stops, and there is no version of safety that does not require you to manage someone else’s experience. You find yourself immersed in codependency symptoms. The way of keeping peace is rarely visible, but it does not mean it’s not real. These symptoms often surface when the peacekeeping role was learned early. This came with knowing that, at any cost, peace must be first.

The Difference Between Peacemaking and Peacekeeping

The kind of Peace that the Bible describes flows from a place of wholeness. “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.” (Matthew 5:9, ESV) The type of peace described there calls for restoration without requiring the peacemaker to disappear in the process.

Peacekeeping has a different narrative. The peacekeeper narrative suggests that there is no harmony, only the illusion of it. Conflict is an anticipated event, so prevention is planned before it even starts. This results in silencing one’s own needs, opinions, and feelings, leading to codependency symptoms.

There’s a gap between what the peacekeeper actually feels and what they allow themselves to express. This is often learned in childhood. Conflict at home felt unpredictable or unsafe, and keeping things calm, staying small, agreeable, or invisible became the default response. The clear lesson was that their comfort matters less than keeping the temperature low. This behavior became instinctive, and by adulthood, it began to feel like part of the person.

Sometimes there’s a grief wrapped up in this realization. The individual who is a peacekeeper may look back and question how many moments they edited themselves out of.

What rooms did they walk into, bracing for what would go wrong? How many relationships were built on the version of themselves that was never quite real? This is the grief that deserves acknowledgment and not just a strategy to move past it. It requires a healing that reaches into the place where peacekeeping took root, done quietly. God is faithful to heal those places in each of us: “He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds.” (Psalm 147:3, ESV)

Codependency Symptoms that Surface in the Peacekeeper

Specific codependency symptoms may appear in people who have made peacekeeping their identity. These individuals often struggle to say no. When this response is required, it often brings feelings of dread at the thought of disappointing someone or creating minor friction. The result is a peacekeeper who says yes when they mean no or agrees when they privately disagree. They are left carrying the weight quietly and still maintaining a calm exterior.

The inability to sit with someone else’s discomfort is another experience of being a peacekeeper. If another person is upset, even if it’s unrelated to the peacekeeper, there is a plan to resolve the situation or stop it. This leads to over-functioning in a relationship and taking ownership of emotions that were not theirs to carry.

Christian counselors identify this as one of the central dynamics of codependency. They emphasize that it shows up with particular intensity in people whose sense of safety is tied to relational harmony.

The erosion of identity happens over time, and the peacekeeper is so practiced at reading and responding that they gradually lose touch with their own interior life. They are unable to define what they want because they have spent so long becoming whatever the room requires.

Resentment also develops over time, though it tends to hide beneath a compliant surface. The peacekeeper gives, adjusts, absorbs, and then wonders why they feel unseen or quietly bitter. The answer is often that they have never given others the chance to truly know them, because they have been too busy becoming whatever the room required.

Where Faith Gets Tangled in the Pattern

Believers who have fallen into the peacekeeper role sometimes encounter the call to servanthood, humility, and a preference for others, since these are genuinely Christian values. However, the main attitudes and social pressures within faith communities reinforced the very behaviors that feed codependency.

This created an unintentional message that sounds like being agreeable does not cause disruption, and the self needs to be set aside for the sake of unity. If a person is already wired toward peacekeeping, this only deepens that groove.

Learning how to separate a healthy, selfless sacrifice from fear-based self-erasure is a balancing act. Christian counselors are trained to identify this type of behavior. Because of the faith-based care, a space is created that allows for honest questions that don’t undermine Scripture but suggest how to apply it with greater clarity. The questions aren’t always comfortable, but they are clarifying and can open the door to something whole.

Moving Through Codependency Symptoms Toward Healing

When codependency symptoms are addressed, it doesn’t mean that unnecessary conflict will start up. It doesn’t stop the peacekeeper from caring about the people around them. The process centers on reclaiming the self that got buried under years of managing everyone else’s experiences. It involves learning to acknowledge feelings that carry weight even when they are inconvenient.

This process requires the individual to practice the uncomfortable art of letting someone else sit with their own distress, resisting the pull to step in and resolve it. It will require patience and self-compassion, as the peacekeeper has spent years operating within this pattern.

Christian counselors have a faith-integrated perspective that allows them to walk alongside people in this work and help them reconnect with who God made them to be before the peacekeeping role took over. Navigating this will lead to discovering that they are not responsible for the emotional climate of every room they enter.

Through the process, the individual learns that healthy limits are not walls that shut people out, but rather boundaries that express love for themselves and the other people in their life. By laying down what was never meant to be carried, you are able to be present, honest, and more capable of lifting others from a place of abundance instead of depletion.

Help for Peacekeeping and Codependency

The weight of a peacekeeper is real, and it does not resolve itself. Codependency symptoms can develop within this role and show up as chronic over-functioning, inability to tolerate another’s distress, or the slow erosion of self within a relationship. These are learned responses to circumstances that once felt out of control. They are not character flaws, and with the right support, they can be gently unlearned.

With the right type of faith-integrated support, these responses can be unlearned as an individual discovers that God does not ask them to disappear for the sake of peace. The pathway to healing includes being honest, grounded, and rooted in who you are as the person God designed you to be.

Grappling with the peacekeeper role can be navigated with the proper support. Contact our reception team, and they can connect you with the support you need for a faith-based approach to the peacekeeper role.

item.title: Curiosity or Dependency? Protecting Yourself From the Trap of AI Delusions and Developing Social Anxiety Disorder
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence is here and here to stay. Without us realizing it, it has already changed the way we live, work, and connect. This technology is now part of daily life, from chat tools to recommendation systems.

While these tools bring convenience, they also create new risks.

One of the fastest-growing concerns is the rise of what some experts have coined as AI delusions, which are false beliefs or distorted perceptions shaped by over-reliance on artificial intelligence. For people already struggling with mental health challenges like social anxiety disorder, this trend is posing an even greater risk and can make daily challenges even harder.

Let’s delve deeper into this and discuss how this AI curiosity can quickly turn into dependency as the first step toward protecting mental health.

Why AI Delusions are Growing so Quickly

AI delusions are not science fiction. They happen when people begin to trust artificial intelligence in ways that blur reality. For example, someone may start believing an AI tool understands their emotions better than friends or family, or they may rely on it for constant reassurance.

These beliefs are growing rapidly because AI systems are designed to respond quickly, mimic human conversation, and provide personalized feedback.

The growth of AI delusions is tied to how accessible these tools have become. They are available on phones, laptops, and even smart home devices. The more people interact with them, the easier it is to slip into thinking they provide more than they really do. Curiosity about new technology is natural, but when curiosity turns into dependency, the risks increase. Overreliance upon AI and isolation leads to living outside of how God has created you, in His image. Fellowship with others, prayer, and community are essentials to a full life, and something that a dependence upon AI cannot satisfy.

Where the Line Gets Blurry

Curiosity is healthy. Trying out new tools, learning how they work, and exploring their benefits is part of adapting to modern life. Dependency, however, is different.

It happens whenever someone begins to rely on anything for emotional support, decision-making, or validation. With AI, the line between curiosity and dependency blurs when the bot starts eliminating actual human connection to unhealthy levels.

For example, checking in with an AI tool for advice once in a while is curiosity. Turning to it every hour of the day for reassurance about personal worth or social interactions can quickly cross the line into dependency. This dependency can quietly grow until it feels normal, making it harder to recognize when habits have become unhealthy.

Not everyone is equally vulnerable to AI delusions. Certain people are more likely to lean on these tools in ways that blur reality.

Who is Most Likely to Fall into the AI Dependency Trap

  • People who already struggle with loneliness or limited social support are at higher risk. When human connection feels difficult or unavailable, AI can seem like a safe substitute.
  • Younger users who grew up with technology also face unique risks. They are comfortable with digital interaction, which makes it easier to slip into believing AI provides genuine companionship.
  • Another group at risk includes individuals under constant pressure, like students, office professionals, or caregivers, who are likely to turn to AI for quick answers and reassurance. Over time, this reliance grows into dependency, especially if they believe the tool understands them better than people around them.
  • Those living with social anxiety disorder are especially vulnerable because interacting with AI feels less stressful than facing real conversations.

The common thread is not weakness, but circumstance. When stress, isolation, or anxiety are present, AI feels like an easy solution. Recognizing these patterns helps explain why the trend is growing so quickly and why awareness is essential. Understanding who is most at risk makes it easier to take steps that protect mental health before dependency deepens.

Common Misconceptions About AI and Mental Health

One misconception is that AI can replace therapy or counseling. While AI tools may provide information or coping tips, they are not trained professionals. Another misconception is that AI understands emotions in the same way humans do. In reality, AI responds based on patterns and data, not genuine empathy.

A third misconception is that using AI for social support is harmless. For someone with social anxiety disorder, relying on AI instead of practicing real-world interactions can reinforce isolation. These misconceptions feed into the growth of AI delusions, making it important to separate fact from fiction.

How AI Delusions Feed into Social Anxiety Disorder

Social anxiety disorder involves fear of judgment, rejection, or embarrassment in social situations. AI delusions can make this worse. When someone believes AI offers safer or more reliable interaction than people, they may withdraw from real relationships. This withdrawal reinforces anxiety, creating a cycle that is hard to break.

AI delusions also feed into distorted thinking. For example, if an AI tool provides constant positive feedback, the person may begin to believe that only AI understands them, increasing anxiety in real social settings, where feedback is more complex and less predictable. Over time, the reliance on AI deepens the disorder instead of helping it.

Examples and Signs Your Relationship with AI Might Be Risky

There are clear signs that curiosity has turned into dependency. These include:

  • Spending more time talking to AI tools than to friends or family
  • Feeling anxious or unsettled when not using AI for reassurance
  • Believing AI understands personal struggles better than people do
  • Avoiding social situations because AI feels safer
  • Relying on AI for decisions that should involve personal judgment or human advice

These signs show that the relationship with AI is no longer balanced. Recognizing them early helps prevent deeper issues.

Simple daily habits help maintain balance.

Daily Habits to Help Keep You Grounded in Reality

  • Limiting time spent with AI tools is one step. Setting aside time for face-to-face conversations, even short ones, reinforces real connection.
  • Writing down personal thoughts in a journal instead of relying on AI for feedback encourages self-reflection.
  • Seeking information from trusted human sources instead of relying solely on AI ensures balanced perspectives.
  • Another helpful habit is practicing mindfulness. Paying attention to real surroundings, sounds, and interactions keeps the mind grounded in reality.
  • Prayer, community, and other methods of expanding social connectedness to assist in being present.
  • Choosing activities that involve creativity, exercise, or nature also reduces dependency on technology.
  • It is also helpful to diversify online activities. Instead of using AI for everything, mix in educational videos, podcasts, or online communities that involve real people.

Such simple, traditional habits we used to take for advantage are the key to helping us remember that fulfillment comes from real experiences, not digital illusions.

Protecting mental health online starts with awareness. Questioning how much time is spent with AI tools and why they are being used is important. Setting boundaries, such as designated offline hours, helps reduce dependency.

This variety reduces the risk of falling into AI delusions and supports healthier online habits.

Seeking Support When AI Disillusionment Turns into Anxiety

When disillusionment with AI or dependency begins to affect your daily life, professional support might be what you need to help steer you right again.

Counselors and life coaches are there to provide guidance in a personal way that AI cannot. They help identify unhealthy patterns, build coping strategies, and encourage real-world connections. For those with social anxiety disorder, professional support is especially important. It provides a safe space to explore fears and develop healthier ways of relating to others.

AI delusions are growing quickly because technology is designed to feel personal and responsive. While curiosity about these tools is natural, dependency creates risks, especially for those living with social anxiety disorder. Recognizing misconceptions, spotting warning signs, and building daily habits that keep life grounded are key steps toward protecting mental health.

If you have realized that your relationship with AI has already become too dependent and your online habits are affecting your well-being, professional help is an important step forward. Counselors and life coaches are available on this site to guide you through these challenges and help you find peace and purpose again.

Contact our office today to speak with our reception team and schedule an appointment with me or another qualified Christian Counselor in our network. You can learn to have a healthier future.

item.title: Choosing Positive Reactions to Manage Stress
item.description:
It’s no secret that life is full of surprises. With technology, bad news travels quickly. Bad news can trigger stress for many people. Stress, in turn, triggers health problems. The general population in America today is becoming more stress-aware. More people are deciding to get healthy and learn to manage stress. By choosing to manage stress, individuals can enhance their quality of life. Stress management tips often include understanding positive reactions.

As Christians, our lifestyle should reflect peace rather than chaos. Chaos can be consuming and destructive not only for ourselves but also for those around us. This is not the life God intends for us. Stress management is a choice that an individual must make to maintain a healthy lifestyle. Worrying does not change anything about circumstances or the outcome; it only changes the way our body and mind feel.

Scripture is clear about the fruitlessness of worry:

And which of you by worrying can add a day to his life’s span? – Luke 12:25, NASB

Knowing the Symptoms of Stress

It’s normal to experience stressful situations in life. Stress can be found on the job, at home, raising kids, going to the grocery store, and even driving in traffic. No one is completely free from experiencing stressful situations. The key thing to remember is that managing stress decreases its effects.

Stress affects a person’s body and mind, which can result in disturbances at work, school, or even at home. To react to stress positively, it’s important to identify the symptoms that come with stress. Here is a short list of the most common symptoms of stress:

  • Constant fatigue
  • Insomnia
  • Digestion issues
  • Headaches
  • Anxiety or panic attacks
  • Mood swings
  • Weight changes
  • Inability to concentrate
  • Fatigue
  • Body tension

All of these symptoms may not be present when experiencing stress, but most of the time, people experience at least five. Whether you experience two symptoms or six, it is still important to understand how to react positively to stress.

Tips for Stress Management

Reacting positively can be done in a multitude of ways. Understanding how to react positively when dealing with stress can decrease the amount of time you spend worrying. Some of the ways to react positively revolve around thought patterns, and others revolve around activities. The following stress management tips can help reduce the effects of stress on the body and mind.

Maintain a dedicated quiet time and read Scripture

Having a dedicated time of day for Bible reading can greatly increase how an individual faces stressful situations. This can also help create mindful quotes that can be recalled when a person is feeling overwhelmed in certain circumstances.

Exercise for fun

Keeping physical activity at the forefront of a daily routine will also help reduce the negative impact of stress. Engaging in exercise in a fun way promotes a more joyful outlook on the situation you may encounter. One of the best ways to make it fun is to include a friend.

Write down the good stuff

Keeping a journal doesn’t have to be mundane and boring. Grab some markers, colors, and fun stickers, and take time to write down the good stuff. Journal about the moments of gratitude you have experienced, and keep track of the inspirational things you’ve seen in a day. These types of things can relieve stress and bring out the best part of the day.

Delight in the pleasures of life

Just as life has stresses, it also has pleasures. Pleasure can come in a variety of ways depending on the person. Take time to enjoy your favorite hobbies or experiences regularly. For instance, camping, sitting around a fire pit, or simply curling up with a good book are pleasures in life that are considered positive reactions to stress.

Set boundaries and reduce negative people

When it comes to positive reactions to stress, it is important to maintain boundaries to reduce negative people or a toxic mindset. Keeping positive people in your life will encourage you to maintain positive reactions while you try to manage stress. This also includes encouraging yourself and having positive self-talk.

Remember it’s okay to laugh

Even though you may be facing a stressful situation, always remember that it’s OK to find humor in the things that happen every day. Learning to find laughter in the middle of stress is one of the best ways to relieve stress, reduce its effects, and find the positive aspects of the situation.

Take on a self-challenge

Sometimes setting a goal or challenge can help with stress management. Trying a new sport can become a way of refocusing your thoughts. An exercise challenge can not only help you refocus, but it will also promote a healthier lifestyle. Consider all kinds of things that could be challenges, then choose ones that appeal to your interests. You could have a reading challenge, a gardening challenge, or even a coffee challenge. The key is to choose something fun and challenge yourself.

Volunteer to help others

Helping others through volunteer work has been proven to reduce stress. By helping others, you create a mindset that encourages positivity. You could also choose a way to brighten someone’s day with a simple gesture of friendship. For instance, picking up an extra cup of coffee in the morning as you head to the office. Doing things for others helps you feel better.

Keep track of the positive things

As you journal each night, you may want to dedicate one page to the positive things of the day. Listing three positive things each day can encourage you to become mindful during the day to look for the positive, even in the middle of a stressful situation.

You can’t change things

One of the most important stress management tips is to realize you can’t always change the situation. There are times when things happen, and we cannot control them. Those are the times we have to realize we do what we can and let the rest go.

Rest is best

The way stress can affect the body can cause a person to lose sleep. To overcome this problem, it’s helpful to have some form of relaxation that will promote a restful night. Cell phones and TV are some of the major contributors to lack of sleep. The suggestion is to turn off the devices and the TV and read a magazine or book to help calm your mind.

Organization brings peace

Wherever your workspace is, it is important to have an organized space. Being able to locate the tools or resources you need to complete a job will reduce the chance of being stressed because of clutter. A home that is clean and organized can also reduce feelings of chaos, not just for you but for the entire family.

Therapy helps

In cases of extreme anxiety, it is beneficial to work with a Christian counselor. This can help identify triggers, understand symptoms, implement techniques, and create a faith-based plan that promotes a positive mindset. It’s OK to realize that sometimes you can’t do it on your own. Getting help from a Christian counselor improves your stress response.

Help for Managing Stress

Learning how to use stress management tips to reduce stress is one of the best ways to react positively to a stressful situation. Remember that a healthy lifestyle, a positive thought process, and understanding your reactions can lead to a lower stress level and better health.

If you or a loved one is struggling with overwhelming stress, reach out to your local Christian counselor. They can help you navigate stress management tips that will work for you. If you’re not sure where to start, the staff in the office can help. Call today to learn how a Christian counselor can help you better manage your stress.

item.title: How to Disclose Infidelity
item.description:
Across the world, emotional and sexual infidelity destroys relationships, leading to breakups or divorces. In the United States alone, it is estimated that 20-40% of relationships are affected by infidelity (Marín, Christensen, & Atkins, 2014). Emotional and sexual infidelity is damaging because it affects self-esteem, causes depression and anxiety, creates attachment injuries, and triggers suicidal ideation in hurt partners.

Frequently, infidelity in relationships leads to significant distress for both partners, especially in the brief period after disclosure or discovery. Hurt partners react in a variety of ways to discovering infidelity: initial shock, wanting to leave, time apart from the offending partner, feeling trapped with no option to leave, or staying and beginning the work to rebuild the relationship.

The Fact of Disclosure

While the consequences are the same for disclosing infidelity to a hurt partner or the hurt partner discovering infidelity, it seems that gentle and thoughtful disclosure is more likely to lead to repair, recovery, and reconciliation between the partners (Simonyi-Gindele & Simonyi-Gindele, 2020).

Involved partners often believe that disclosing infidelity is the harmful part. However, the infidelity itself does the real damage to the hurt partner (Simonyi-Gindele & Simonyi-Gindele). If the offending partner validates the hurt partner’s sense of reality, the disclosure will go more easily. As described above, the hurt partner will experience a gamut of emotions. Emotionally, hurt partners will feel like their entire world has collapsed around them.

There are a few exceptions to a gentle, thoughtful disclosure. The first exception is when the hurt partner has expressed an imminent, verifiable threat to harm the involved partner if he or she discloses infidelity.

In those special circumstances, preventive law enforcement intervention and involvement would be strongly advised before disclosure. The offending partner may choose to keep it secret or divorce the hurt partner as an alternative. Not disclosing infidelity in these cases leads to superficial emotional intimacy.

The second exception applies to individuals with a sex addiction. Since there are likely multiple sex partners and infidelities, the process is more complex than a simple thoughtful disclosure (Schneder et al., 1998). In addition, the hurt partner is likely aware of the involved partner’s dalliances (Schneder et al.). Individuals with a sex addiction may require advanced mental health care at an inpatient program specializing in sexual addiction and betrayal.

The Process of Disclosure

Schneder and associates concluded that disclosure is often a process, not a one-time event. However, disclosure should not be staggered. It is best to get everything in the open, as described below. Nevertheless, we are human and tend to forget some details, especially if we do not have support to remind us.

Second, they reminded us that the initial disclosure is usually the make-or-break point to healing the relationship in the long run, including all the major elements of the acting-out behaviors. Initial disclosure does not involve the “gory details.” The “gory details” are sexual positions used by the offending and affair partners and anything that enhanced the romance, i.e., perfume, adult toys, and lingerie, between them.

Third, they recommend that both partners need support from professionals and peers during the process of disclosure. When the involved partner chooses to disclose infidelity to his or her partner, it is advisable to gather all the information possible. Although heart-rending, disclosure is best when it delivers everything in one swift and painful blow.

The offending partner must have a support system in place. The support system will keep the involved partner from leaving out any details. Offending partners are often anxious when disclosing information to the hurt partner. For the hurt partner, a support system will help him or her sort his or her feelings objectively, weigh the pros and cons, give the hurt partner the pros and cons, and help guide the recovery process.

Disclosing Details of Infidelity

If details are left out, the disclosure becomes staggered disclosure. Staggered disclosure causes further injury because it rips the scab off a healing wound. Staggered disclosure requires as much work as discovery of infidelity to rebuild trust with the hurt partner. The hurt partner asks him or herself questions, such as “What is next?” “What did my partner leave out?” “Is my partner truly remorseful?” or “Is my partner trying to weasel out of natural and logical consequences?

In addition to a support system, the involved partners need to be prepared to answer all the hurt questions. The most important questions are:

  • who the affair partner was
  • when the affair began and ended
  • how many separate acts of infidelity occurred
  • what made the affair partner different than the hurt partner
  • whether there was safe sex
  • whether the offending partner was in love with the affair partner
  • whether the affair partner and the involved partner were treated for STDs
  • whether contact with the affair partner has ended
  • whether a child was conceived during the affair
  • why the offending partner is choosing to return to the hurt partner

This writer believes that two particular questions are strictly off-limits for the hurt partner to ask: 1) which sex positions were used during the affair, and 2) whether items were used to spice up the affair, i.e., lingerie, perfume, adult toys, etc. Both questions tend to retraumatize hurt partners as they visualize these acts or scenes repeatedly in their minds.

When disclosing infidelity, especially when done without a mental health professional present, disclosure needs to be slow and in bite-sized pieces. The hurt partner will likely be quite hurt and will need time to absorb everything.

Thus, it is advisable to allow a minimum of two to three hours to disclose the infidelity. Allowing plenty of time gives the hurt partner time to absorb the information emotionally and take appropriate breaks to prevent flooding of emotions. It is important to reveal everything in one session.

Considerations When Disclosing Infidelity

When disclosing infidelity, it is important to be empathetic toward the hurt partner. The involved partner must place him or herself in the shoes of the hurt partner. Second, the offending partner must not pass judgment on the hurt partner or minimize his or her actions. Third, the involved partner must recognize all the emotions the hurt partner is experiencing. Fourth, the offending partner must communicate the understanding of the hurt partner’s emotions by validating them.

It is guaranteed that the hurt partner will have some strong emotions. It is wise for the involved partner not to treat the hurt partner’s emotions as an overreaction. Likewise, it would be detrimental to tell the hurt partner how to feel. As described above, the hurt partner will feel blindsided, shocked, confused, grieved, and emotionally kicked in the stomach.

It is unrealistic to believe that forgiveness happens instantaneously, like taking a magic pill that erases all harm done. In cases of infidelity, the offending partner must apologize for the infidelity.

However, it is completely delusional to believe that forgiveness takes place immediately. When infidelity is disclosed, validating the hurt partner’s pain, accepting responsibility, laying out a recovery plan, seeking individual treatment beforehand, and taking steps before disclosing, i.e., switching jobs to move away from an affair partner/co-worker, goes a long way for the hurt partner.

In addition to the three requirements above, trust must be rebuilt. Trust involves honesty, transparency, reliability, and security. Security is the subjective quality of feeling safe. No objective standard can measure security. Reliability means being willing to be held liable again and again. An offending partner in infidelity says something and follows through with it.

Transparency means everything is visible and can be inspected by the hurt partner. The involved partner does not try to hide anything from the hurt partner. Honesty means being truthful, even when it hurts. Deception and manipulation of the hurt partner do not occur.

Regardless of whether the infidelity was disclosed or discovered, the reconciliation process will be excruciating for both partners. Infidelity recovery includes evaluating the damage to the relationship, rebuilding trust, reestablishing commitment between partners, creäting and maintaining accountability, learning to communicate more deeply, and developing true forgiveness (Fife et al., 2023).

Next Steps

Often, when rebuilding a relationship plagued by infidelity, couples require forgiveness and seek professional help. An educated, Christian counselor can teach clients how to forgive each other, help them manage painful and recurring memories, assist the couple with their changing couple-dynamics, and modify power dynamics within their relationship.

At Spokane Christian Counseling, we have many counselors who have walked alongside countless clients to restore relationships and help them start on the path of recovery and reconciliation.

item.title: Anxiety in the Bible: How to Move from Worry Toward Rest
item.description:
We often try to ground our sense of peace in things that can change in an instant. We look to our health, financial stability, our friendships and other relationships, our looks, and other areas for peace. These things can have benefits in their own way, but they ultimately form a poor foundation for life because they aren’t permanent.

If we want something that will stand the test of time, a foundation upon which to build our lives that will survive the fiercest assaults that life can launch against us, such a hope and such a foundation can only be found in Jesus. This has remarkable implications for our lives, including the sense of security we can have, knowing that we are safe in Christ, even when we go through tough times.

Anxiety is a normal reaction to stress as a potential danger. We need a way to protect ourselves against harm, and so our bodies have the remarkable ability to prepare for such instances. Our fight-or-flight response, which is triggered by stress and danger (whether real or imagined), prepares our body to respond appropriately to the situation. This could be a job interview, a first date, or a snake that just slithered across your path.

While feeling a bit of anxiety can be a normal response in stressful situations, such as a public speaking engagement or taking a test, those feelings of anxiety can also function as an indicator of something deeper. It’s important to notice when they become excessive, all-consuming, and begin interfering with your day-to-day life. In those cases, anxiety has become a disorder, and that is a condition diagnosable by a mental health professional.

If you find that your anxiety is out of control and undermining your well-being and daily functioning, you should consider going to a mental health professional for a proper diagnosis.

Thankfully, the Lord has not left us without wisdom and guidance regarding anxiety or any other part of our lives. Treatment for anxiety includes psychotherapy and medication. Part of what happens in psychotherapy is talking with your therapist. They can help you begin understanding the causes of anxiety, your triggers for anxiety, and any patterns of thought, behavior, and action that undermine your well-being.

These unhealthy and unhelpful patterns of behavior and thinking need to be understood and ultimately replaced by healthier ones. Part of how you can deal with everyday anxiety, as well as deeper anxiety disorders, is to speak God’s truths over yourself. You can begin to pattern your thinking and being in ways that align with God’s truth and ways.

Below are some Scriptures that can help us work through our anxiety and ground us in the hope, security, and freedom from fear that can only come through Jesus Christ.

Come and find rest

“Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.” – Matthew 11:28–30, ESV

Jesus invites people to place their trust in him and place their lives in his hands. For those who are carrying the burden of religious legalism, Jesus invites you to set it down. Instead of being weighed down by the laws that seemed to multiply guilt without necessarily offering any relief, Jesus offers rest for our souls.

This means that He is offering freedom from the crushing burden of guilt of trying to earn salvation by good works to those who desire eternal rest and seek forgiveness of their sins.

Sometimes, we are anxious in life because we feel like we don’t measure up to a standard, whether it is that of the people around us or to God’s standards. Jesus frees us from that by offering us the lighter burden of being his disciples and finding rest through simple commitment to him.

We live for Him, and He loves, cares for, and accepts us already. We pursue our life in Him from the position of knowing we are already loved and accepted, and we don’t have to earn it because Jesus has done it for us on the cross.

When good things become ultimate things that take us off course, it can make us anxious as we try to keep it all together. In our culture, we are consumed by many anxieties and concerns, and these have become ultimate for many of us. When things like our safety, our personal health, or the environment and its viability become ultimate concerns, the enormity of the problems, coupled with our limited capacities, makes us feel endlessly fragile and anxious.

What we need is to bring things back into perspective and make God the center of our lives. That way, these other things begin to occupy their proper place. When we yield to Jesus and his yoke, it allows us to approach these good concerns with the resources and wisdom of God, and that can help us find peace and rest. We can trust that our work in the Lord will not be in vain (1 Corinthians 15: 58). We don’t need to feel anxious about our impact or how things will unfold.

Finding Peace in Hard Places

The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want. He makes me lie down in green pastures. He leads me beside still waters. He restores my soul. He leads me in paths of righteousness for his name’s sake. Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil,
for you are with me; your rod and your staff, they comfort me. – Psalm 23:1-4, ESV

Fear is probably the strongest human emotion, and we often agonize over all the challenging and dreadful things that could happen to us at any moment. This includes what might happen to our health and finances, losing our loved ones, failing at something important, or being rejected.

Life is often not safe, and we never know what we can find in the hard things we go through. Many things can bring suspense and danger in our lives. These verses from Psalm 23 are a good reminder that the people of God have assurance that God is with them in those times, and so they need not fear. God draws us to find rest and restoration when we follow and trust him.

Trusting In God’s Provision and Care

And he said to his disciples, “Therefore I tell you, do not be anxious about your life, what you will eat, nor about your body, what you will put on. For life is more than food, and the body more than clothing.

“Consider the ravens: they neither sow nor reap, they have neither storehouse nor barn, and yet God feeds them. Of how much more value are you than the birds! And which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to his span of life? If then you are not able to do as small a thing as that, why are you anxious about the rest?” –  Luke 12:22-26, ESV

There are many reasons why believers should not be anxious, and several of them are given in this passage from Luke. For one thing, our lives are more than what we eat; even our bodies are more than what we eat. We do need food and clothing, but these things enable us to focus on what life is really about: loving God and loving our neighbor. It’s challenging, but we can love God and our neighbor whether we are well-fed or not.

If our lives are preoccupied by the means and not the ends of our lives, we can be consumed by the pressure to gather the things that seemingly secure our existence, so much so that we miss the point. Believers also shouldn’t be anxious because they realize how much value they possess in God’s eyes. If he cares for birds, why wouldn’t he care for you?

Anxiety is also not in our best interests because none of us has enough control over our own life, even to add a single hour to our span of life. It’s quite counterintuitive, but striving and taking things into our own hands, and then getting anxious because life is not under our control, doesn’t help us. It is far better to surrender ourselves to the loving care of our heavenly Father, who does have everything under control.

Important Reminders

Psalm 56 reminds us that “When I am afraid, I put my trust in you.” (Psalm 56:3, NIV) We can try to put our trust elsewhere, but those things will ultimately fail and disappoint us. This will likely lead us into deeper anxiety and worry as we try to secure ourselves against the hardships we face in life.

Writing nearly seventeen centuries ago, in his long prayer called Confessions, Augustine wrote, “You have made us for yourself, O Lord, and our hearts are restless until they rest in you.” (Augustine) Our restless and anxious hearts try to find peace and rest in many ways, but we can only find what we are looking for in the Lord. This is our deepest need.

To deal with our anxiety, we should be aware of this need and where to have it met. We can grow in our awareness of our unhealthy patterns of behavior and thought through therapy and with the assistance, when necessary, of medication to ease the symptoms of anxiety. This can help us function in life. If you’re ready to learn more about therapy for anxiety, contact this office for more information.

item.title: Stress Eating: What Causes It and How to Overcome It
item.description:
Food, glorious food. The Lord has blessed us with many things, one of which is food. After blessing the first humans and commissioning them to be faithful stewards over His creation, the Lord instructed them on where to find food, a necessity for their survival (Genesis 1:28-30). Then we read, “God saw all that he had made, and it was very good” (Genesis 1:31, NIV). Food is a part of that “very good”.

However, it would be painting a skewed picture to leave matters at that. The Fall of humanity occurred, and our connection to the Lord, ourselves, each other, and between ourselves and the non-human created world was severely disrupted (Genesis 3). As Paul puts it, the creation is in “bondage to decay” (Romans 8:21, NIV). One implication is that our bodies and food may not naturally be in a harmonious relationship.

Stress eating is one of the ways we can relate to food and ourselves in an unhealthy and unbalanced way. Understanding what stress eating is, why we do it, how it affects us, and the ways to overcome it can help you manage life challenges more constructively.

Stress Eating in Brief

Commonly, we often talk about comfort eating, but it is also referred to as stress eating or emotional eating. One reason the term ‘emotional eating’ can be helpful is that it leaves room for the different emotional states that could be at the root of why we’re eating to satisfy something other than our hunger. A person can ‘eat’ their feelings, and that includes emotional states such as anxiety, sadness, or stress.

When a person eats to cope with their stress or other emotional states, that’s marked by a few characteristics. Typically, they will crave comfort foods. These are foods that are high in salt, fat, or sugar content. Stress eating is about using food as a coping mechanism, and often, the eating is not about satisfying hunger. Another characteristic is that there’s often a loss of control, making it hard to stop or limit one’s food intake.

As the eating isn’t strictly related to physical hunger, stress eating will often lead a person past satiation. This can cause significant health issues in the short term as well as down the line.

Why We Stress Eat

Stress eating can be a huge challenge, and to tackle it, you need to understand why we turn to food to relieve emotional distress. Several factors may be at play to explain why we stress eat. Stress eating is about using food to manage feelings of stress. In other words, food functions as a coping mechanism to manage the unpleasantness of stress, sadness, or anxiety.

Stress releases the hormone cortisol, and that hormonal response can increase one’s appetite and cravings for comfort food. Depending on the type and duration of stress, stress can activate the brain’s reward system, making you more sensitive to rewards like dopamine, which make comfort foods appealing. Stress eating feels good, providing temporary relief or comfort from stressors.

We also stress eat because it’s something we’ve learned to do. Foods high in sugar, fat, and salt activate the brain’s reward system, which releases dopamine, and then we begin to associate those foods with pleasure. These foods become associated with positive emotions and memories connected with relaxation, comfort, or feeling good. It increases the likelihood of stress eating at a future date.

Another factor that also makes it likely to stress eat is the lack of other, healthier coping mechanisms. If you don’t have other stress-management techniques handy, it may be easier to turn to food for a quick fix.

The combination of environmental, biological, and emotional factors may make it challenging to resist your cravings for comfort foods when you’re experiencing stress or other difficult emotional states. Though stress eating can provide you with temporary relief, ultimately, it may lead to negative consequences such as unplanned weight gain, feelings of guilt, or worsened mental health.

How Stress Eating Affects You

On that note, highlighting how stress eating affects you can provide you with important information about the cost of stress eating. Pointing out the negative effects of stress eating isn’t necessarily enough to turn things around, but it can be helpful. Naming these effects can, for instance, help you to identify and process your experiences after stress eating. Stress eating can affect you emotionally, mentally, physically, and relationally.

One of the ways that stress eating affects an individual includes impacting their physical health. It can lead to digestive issues, particularly when you eat beyond feeling full, and it can result in unplanned weight gain. With weight gain come other concerns, such as decreased mobility and an increased risk of chronic diseases such as diabetes, high blood pressure, and cardiac disease.

Stress eating can also affect your emotional well-being. When you stress-eat, the lack of control and sheer excess of it all can lead to feelings of guilt and shame. You may even become anxious about your eating habits and what they are doing to you. Stress eating can worsen conditions like anxiety and depression, impacting your mental health as well.

How you perceive yourself matters. Feelings of guilt or shame from stress eating may result in low confidence or a negative self-image. When your self-esteem takes a knock, that can affect how you perform and are in your relationships, at work, and in other contexts. This may, in turn, fuel further distress, which can turn into emotional eating to cope, feeding a seemingly endless cycle.

Another possible effect of stress eating is that it can affect your relationships. Dealing with conflict by stress eating won’t resolve matters; it may result in deepening the conflict. If a person hides their stress eating, that can also introduce strain into the relationship. The cycle of emotional distress that stress eating can create makes it harder to manage emotions and stress effectively. This can make conducting a healthy relationship more challenging.

Managing and Overcoming Stress Eating

When you recognize the impact of stress eating on your life, that could be a good first step toward seeking help and cultivating healthier coping mechanisms that won’t undermine your well-being. Some of the strategies that can effectively help you to manage and overcome stress eating include the following:

Identify triggers Whether through journaling or reflection, it’s possible to identify and learn to recognize the emotions, situations, events, or experiences that lead to stress eating. Perhaps for you it’s a hard workday, or it could be a relationship conflict that leads to stress eating. Maybe it’s having tight deadlines or struggling to connect with loved ones. Keeping a food diary may help you track your habits.

Eat regular, balanced meals When you eat regularly and your meals are balanced, this can help you reduce cravings and maintain relatively stable levels of energy. Good nutrition helps your emotional, mental, and physical well-being, which can all contribute to better emotional regulation. Doing this requires planning, including having healthy snacks and meals available to avoid eating impulsively.

Practice mindful eating Mindfulness is all about being fully present in whatever situation you’re in. When you’re mindful about your eating, you pay attention to cues such as whether you’re hungry or full, eat your food slowly instead of wolfing it down, and take the time to savor your food and the process of preparing it. These are small ways to build a healthy relationship with your food.

Develop self-care habits Making self-care a priority, whether that’s getting enough sleep, doing regular exercise, spending time with loved ones, doing hobbies, or taking time to rest and relax, all helps to reduce stress levels. The more you perform and enjoy these activities, the easier it’ll be to turn to them in times of stress instead of to food for comfort.

Challenge your thoughts There’s a place for challenging your negative thoughts, particularly the ones that can lead you toward food as a source of comfort. Whether it’s thoughts encouraging one more bite or thoughts that are self-disparaging, they can and should be challenged. Apply what you know is true to address your emotional eating patterns and nurture a healthy relationship with yourself and your food.

Seek support and professional help Don’t suffer in silence about stress or your eating habits. Embarrassment, guilt, or shame shouldn’t stand in the way of your seeking the help you need. Talk to wise and trusted loved ones about what you’re going through. You can also consult professionals, whether a registered dietitian or nutritionist, or a counselor who can give you guidance in addressing harmful thought patterns.

“So whether you eat or drink or whatever you do, do it all for the glory of God” (2 Corinthians 10:31, NIV). It’s possible to develop a healthier relationship with your food and to deal with stress and other emotions effectively without turning to food for comfort. Reach out for help from a professional to start that journey. Contact our office today to learn more.

item.title: What is Depression? A Christian Counselor in Spokane, WA Explains
item.description:
I have worked with many clients who suffer from depression too, and I found myself always needing more information about what exactly depression is. I have known family members who have struggled with it, as well as friends and colleagues over the years.

So, I determined to take a medium dive into the literature to see if I could feel at the end of that journey that I could put my arms around what depression is, what its causes are, and what some viable treatments are. This is the first of three parts that cover the subject.

As I began to read from several academically reviewed sources, the journey did not really land on solid ground. I still feel that depression is like this fog or mist from a Stephen King novel that covers everything and that we don’t know about it. It lurks out there as an invisible impending threat.

We have all been through times when we felt emotionally down without explanation or that things were so stressful that we felt destined to fail at whatever challenge was ahead. Or, as life can be, we have been dealt some serious losses.

Freud said that depression (he called it melancholia) “is an affective disorder characterized by a deeply painful mood, a loss of interest in the outside world, a loss of ability to love, the inhibition of every achievement and the lowering of self-esteem, which manifests itself in self-reproach and self-abuse” (Leuzinger-Bohleber et. al. p. 1). Sounds familiar, doesn’t it?

Essentially, depression is a persistent low mood that affects most areas of one’s life and shapes the way one interprets the world in which they live. Depression is a serious mental illness, and it is not a sign of a weakling state or some character flaw. In ancient civilizations, the common view of depression was that people who were depressed for extended periods had spiritual problems.

The Greeks thought that causeless depression was due to internal body fluids like bile. In the 18th and 19th centuries, these ideas persisted, and some other theories emerged, but the treatment of these folks was horrific. Such things as being locked into asylums, bloodletting, immersion into water for as long as one could stand, and spinning stools, to name a few.

In the 19th and 20th centuries, such ideas as electroshock and lobotomies were introduced. I mention this past to put into perspective where we are today. We have a greater understanding of the ramifications or symptoms of depression, as well as having made much progress in treatments.

Prevalence

If misery loves company, then there is a lot of company among the depressed in our modern world. As of September 2025, the percentage of adults who reported being depressed in their lifetime at least once was 28.5%. For adolescents and young adults, the prevalence was almost 20%, and 8.3% had had at least one major depressive episode. There is consistent research over the past several decades that females are more likely than males to have depression.

For the elderly, the numbers are difficult to assess and are likely undiagnosed because people tend to think their symptoms are normal for their age. One report found that almost 50% of older folks in nursing homes displayed depressive symptoms. I suspect this phenomenon with the elderly speaks to some of our societal flaws. About 36% of depressed elderly folks receive any treatment for their condition and are less likely to receive treatment as they get older.

From my days as a Marriage and Family Therapy graduate student, I focused on the elderly and discovered the suicide rate for that group is high and likely way underreported. This is likely due to not knowing if an overdose of meds was intentional or not. And shockingly, most completed suicides were with firearms.

Major Depressive Disorder and its qualifying symptoms serve as a marker for gathering data on the prevalence of depression among groups of people. Though many people can experience a single episode, there is consistent research that shows that most people who have one episode are 50-80% more likely to have another episode in their life.

Teens are vulnerable to depression. There are many reasons for this, but it seems obvious that social media immersion has contributed to the greater occurrence. About 18% of adolescents aged 12-17 have had a major depressive episode.

Adolescents are keenly aware of their standing in their world and are often hypersensitive – they always have been. What’s more important than being cool? It doesn’t take much to send a teen down the rabbit hole of insecurity of their self.

The sadness that comes from depression is most often rooted in a negative self-evaluation. No doubt, certain circumstances in life can get one down. Financial stress, unemployment, death of a loved one, or any misfortune outside of oneself can easily be turned inward. These troubles become difficult to process, and though they seem to come from outside yourself, you reason that an internal flaw can better explain the troubles.

“In depression, what feels lost or damaged is part of oneself” (McWilliam, p 234). Common statements by the depressed have been “I’m not good enough, I’m flawed, I’m self-indulgent, I’m evil” (p. 235).

The poor soul is driven to take an inward look and doesn’t like what he/she sees. “Depressive people are agonizingly aware of every sin they have committed, every kindness they have neglected to extend, every selfish inclination that has crossed their minds.” (p. 239).

The sources of these thoughts are legion. They are often a result of how they have perceived others’ responses to them, often from an early age. The seed of self-doubt and self-disappointment or loathing often comes from the adults in their lives who sent that message or valued peers who seem to hold a grip over their sense of self-worth.

Some inexplicable sources for depression could connect to biology/genetics or a combination of factors. We will delve into this in part two of this series.

Symptoms

Before I share the clinical diagnostic symptoms for depression, it’s important to know that several physical symptoms can be attributed to depression. Depression affects the body. Many folks experience unexplained aches and pains in the muscles or joints. If there is a chronic pain issue, it could get worse. Many have complained of back pain or headaches.

Perpetual fatigue is common even when getting enough sleep. Sleep is often disturbed by either insomnia or hypersomnia. While depressed, there is often the experience of eating binges and gaining weight, and conversely, loss of appetite and significant weight loss. Gastrointestinal issues are also common.

There are often changes in one’s physical movement, being either slowed down or agitated. In addition to these marked symptoms is a reduction in sexual drive. The point is that depression adversely affects the whole person, not just the mind.

The DSM 5 (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders) is the common tool to determine a given mental disorder. The keyword is “disorder.” To qualify, the disturbance needs to negatively impact one or more aspects of one’s life. The description of the disorder makes no statement of judgment, does not imply cause, nor does it offer treatment. The following is word for word from the of the DSM 5 regarding Major Depressive Disorder (MDD).

1. Five (or more) of the following symptoms have been present during the same week period and represent a change from previous functioning; at least one of the symptoms is (1) depressed mood or (2) loss of interest or pleasure.

2. Depressed mood most of the day, nearly every day, as indicated by either subjective report (e.g., feels sad, empty, hopeless) or observation made by others (note: in children and adolescents, can be irritable mood.

3. Markedly diminished interest in pleasure in all, or almost all, activities most of the day, nearly every day (as indicated by either subjective account or observation)

4. Significant weight loss when not dieting or weight gain (e.g., a change of more than 5% of body weight in a month) or decrease or increase in appetite nearly every day.

5. Insomnia or hypersomnia nearly every day.

6. Psychomotor agitation or retardation nearly every day (observable by others, not merely subjective feeling or restlessness or being slowed down).

7. Fatigue or loss of energy nearly every day

8. Feelings of worthlessness or excessive or inappropriate guilt (which may be delusional) nearly every day (not merely self-reproach or guilt about being sick).

9. Diminished ability to concentrate, or indecisiveness, nearly every day (either by subjective account or as observed by others).

10. Recurrent thoughts of death (not just fear of dying), recurrent suicidal ideation without a specific plan, or a suicide attempt or a specific plan for committing suicide.

11. The symptoms cause clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning.

12. The episode is not attributable to the physiological effects of a substance or other medical condition.

American Psychiatric Association. (2022). Diagnostic and statistical manual of mental disorders (5th ed., text rev.). https://doi.org/10.1176/appi.books.9780890425787 [1]

There is another diagnostic resource known as the International Classification System for Diseases (ICD) that mirrors most of the symptom criteria that is in the DSM 5. Specifically, the diagnostic code is ICD-10 for major depressive disorder.

Depression can be a persistent condition as well. In major depressive disorder, the condition can come and then leave for a time or never come back. But Persistent Depressive Disorder, sometimes referred to as dysthymia, is a condition that lasts two years or more. The criteria for PDD are much like MDD. One of the characteristics is that it is resistant to treatment and is considered a more severe condition.

The symptoms of these illnesses are serious and should not be ignored by the one experiencing them or those who might witness them. Depression is not a condition in which you can just exhort the person to snap out of it, pull themselves up, or tell them to think differently.

There are several theories about the causes of this illness, but it should not be treated any differently than if someone has diabetes or a heart condition or any other disease where we don’t judge the character of someone for having it.

The symptoms can be on a spectrum of mild to severe, so keep that in mind as you consider how you are feeling or as you consider someone else. If you or someone you care about is experiencing these symptoms as listed above. Please feel free to contact me at 509-569-7102 or email me at martyr@spokaneschristiancounseling.com.

If you feel your safety or the safety of someone you care about is in jeopardy, please call 988 or 911 immediately to get appropriate help.
